props.title: Obsession
props.initialSlug: Man falls for wife's lookalike in Hitchcockian thriller

sections.content: Brian De Palma's Obsession (1976) stands as a masterful Hitchcockian thriller that demonstrates the director's virtuosic command of psychological suspense. Drawing clear inspiration from Vertigo (1958), De Palma crafts a haunting meditation on grief, identity, and romantic fixation. The film's dreamlike atmosphere, enhanced by Bernard Herrmann's final and perhaps most emotionally charged score, creates an unsettling exploration of one man's inability to process trauma. Like De Palma's later work Body Double (1984), it showcases his signature split-screen techniques and elaborate camera movements that heighten the psychological tension.

sections.content: The 1970s marked a crucial period for psychological thrillers that explored themes of obsession and doppelgangers. Films like The Passenger (1975) and Sisters (1972) challenged audience perceptions of identity and reality. De Palma's work during this era, particularly Obsession, demonstrates how the American New Wave directors reinterpreted classical Hollywood techniques through a more psychologically complex lens. The film's star Cliff Robertson delivers a performance that echoes James Stewart's haunted detective in Vertigo (1958), while adding layers of post-Vietnam American masculine anxiety.

Cinematographer Vilmos Zsigmond's ethereal photography in Obsession creates a dreamy, almost ghostly atmosphere that would influence later films about grief and memory like In the Cut (2003) and Birth (2004). The film's New Orleans setting provides a gothic backdrop that enhances themes of history repeating itself, while Paul Schrader's screenplay explores the dark intersection of love and madness that he would later revisit in Cat People (1982). sections.content: While Obsession most directly references Vertigo (1958), it represents De Palma's most profound engagement with Hitchcock's themes rather than just his techniques. Unlike the more playful homages in Dressed to Kill (1980) or Body Double (1984), Obsession digs deeper into the psychological implications of Hitchcock's work. The film's elaborate plot twists serve not just as thriller elements but as expressions of deep-seated trauma and guilt, aspects that would influence later psychological thrillers like Mulholland Drive (2001) and Black Swan (2010).
